questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.topic: Distance from a point to a plane
questions.learningObjective: interpret the point-to-plane distance as a projection of the offset
questions.stem: How is the distance from a point to a plane obtained from the plane's equation?

options.text: Substitute the point into the plane's left side and divide by the normal's length
Substitute the point into the plane's left side and keep the value as the distance
options.misconception: believes the raw substitution gives the distance without normalising

options.text: Add the point's coordinates and divide by the number of variables in the plane
options.misconception: believes distance depends only on how many coordinates the point has

options.text: Take the square root of the substituted value so that negative results stay real
options.misconception: believes a square root is needed to make a signed offset a distance

questions.explanation: Writing the plane as the zero set of a linear form, the form evaluated at a point measures displacement along the normal direction, so the perpendicular distance is that value in absolute value divided by the length of the normal vector. The division is essential because the form's value scales with the size of the normal, and no square root is involved at all, since the expression is already a projection length.
questions.hint: Think of the linear form as measuring signed displacement in the normal direction.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.topic: Distance from a point to a line
questions.learningObjective: compute the distance from a point to a line in the plane
questions.stem: What is the distance from the point (2, −1) to the line whose equation is 5x − 3y − 4 = 0? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The distance is the absolute value of the left side at the point, which is 10 plus 3 minus 4, that is 9, divided by the length of the normal ⟨5, −3⟩, which is the root of 34, giving about 1.5435. The check is geometric: the foot of the perpendicular is the point (2, −1) minus 9 over 34 times the normal, which is (0.676, −0.206), and the length of that offset vector is the same 1.5435.
questions.hint: Substitute the point, then divide by the length of the normal vector.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.topic: Angle between a line and a plane
questions.learningObjective: explain why the line-to-plane angle is the complement of the line-to-normal angle
questions.stem: A line meets a plane at a visible angle. How is that angle obtained from the angle between the line and the plane's normal vector?

options.text: It is the complement of the angle the line makes with the normal, the sine of that angle
It is the same as the angle the line makes with the normal, since both meet at once
options.misconception: believes the angle with the plane and with its normal coincide

options.text: It is the angle the line makes with the normal divided by the length of the normal
options.misconception: believes the angle is recovered by dividing one angle by a length

options.text: It is twice the angle the line makes with the normal, since the line crosses both faces
options.misconception: believes meeting two perpendicular surfaces doubles the angle

questions.explanation: A line that lies in the plane makes a zero angle with it but a right angle with the normal, and a line perpendicular to the plane makes a right angle with it and a zero angle with the normal, so the two angles always add to a right angle. That is why the sine of the angle between the line and the plane equals the absolute value of the line-normal dot product divided by the product of their lengths.
questions.hint: Test the formula on a line that lies in the plane and on one normal to it.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.topic: Distance from a point to a plane
questions.learningObjective: compute the distance from a point to a plane in three dimensions
questions.stem: What is the distance from the point (1, 2, 3) to the plane x + 2y − z = 0? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The left side at the point is 1 + 4 − 3 = 2, and the normal ⟨1, 2, −1⟩ has length √6, so the distance is 2 over √6, about 0.8165. Since the point satisfies neither a sign restriction nor anything unusual, and the formula gives a positive value here, the absolute value was unnecessary in this instance but would have been needed had the offset been negative.
questions.hint: Evaluate the plane's left side at the point and divide by the normal's length.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.learningObjective: identify the axis of a circular cylinder from its equation
questions.stem: The surface x squared plus y squared equal to 16 is drawn. What kind of surface is it, and along which line does it extend?

options.text: A circular cylinder of radius 4, whose axis is the whole z-axis
A circular cylinder of radius 4, whose axis is the line x equal to y in that plane
options.misconception: believes the axis of a cylinder is a diagonal inside its cross-section

options.text: A circular sphere of radius 4, centred at the origin of that plane
options.misconception: believes a missing squared term still describes a closed surface

options.text: A circular cone of base radius 4, whose axis is the line through the origin of that plane
options.misconception: believes a circular cross-section that does not shrink can be a cone

questions.explanation: A cylinder is the set of points at a fixed distance from a line, and here that distance is 4 from the z-axis, with no condition at all involving the third coordinate, so the surface is unbounded along the z-axis. A sphere would need the sum of all three squared coordinates to be fixed, and a cone would need the cross-section to shrink, which nothing in this equation does.
questions.hint: Ask which coordinate is missing from the equation, since the surface is invariant along it.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.learningObjective: find the angle between two planes from their normal vectors
questions.stem: Find the acute angle in degrees between the planes z equal to 0 and x + y + z equal to 0. Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The normals are ⟨0, 0, 1⟩ and ⟨1, 1, 1⟩, so the cosine of the angle between the planes is the absolute dot product 1 divided by 1 times √3, which is 1 over √3, and the angle is 54.7356 degrees. The check is that the second normal makes the same angle with the z-axis as a vector with equal horizontal components, whose angle above the horizontal plane is the arctangent of √2, matching this value.
questions.hint: Take the angle between the normals, using the smaller of the two supplementary angles.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.learningObjective: identify the vertex of a circular cone from its equation
questions.stem: The surface z equal to x squared plus y squared is drawn. What kind of surface is it, and where is its vertex?

options.text: A circular cone opening upward, whose vertex is the point (0, 0, 0)
A circular cone opening downward, whose vertex is far along the negative z-axis
options.misconception: believes the sign of z in the equation fixes which way the cone opens

options.text: A paraboloid opening upward, whose vertex is the point (0, 0, 0)
options.misconception: believes a linear right-hand side still gives a paraboloid

options.text: A circular cylinder, whose axis is the z-axis and whose vertex is at the origin
options.misconception: believes any surface with circular cross-sections is a cylinder

questions.explanation: The cross-section at height z has radius the root of z, which shrinks to nothing exactly at z = 0, and that single point where the surface comes to a point is the vertex, so the surface is a cone opening in the positive z direction. A paraboloid would need the right-hand side to be linear in the horizontal coordinates, and a cylinder would need the right-hand side to be constant.
questions.hint: Find the point where the horizontal cross-section shrinks to nothing.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.topic: Angle between a line and a plane
questions.learningObjective: compute the angle at which a line meets a plane
questions.stem: A line has direction ⟨1, 1, 1⟩ and meets the plane z equal to 0. Find the angle in degrees between the line and the plane. Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The normal is ⟨0, 0, 1⟩, so the sine of the angle between the line and the plane is the absolute dot product 1 divided by √3 times 1, and the angle whose sine is that is 35.2644 degrees. Reading the dot product as a cosine would give 54.7356 degrees instead, which is the angle to the normal, and the two are complementary as they must be.
questions.hint: Use the sine, not the cosine, of the line-to-normal dot product, then invert.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.learningObjective: distinguish the tube radius of a torus from the distance to its axis
questions.stem: A torus is built by revolving a circle of radius 3 about a coplanar axis whose distance from the circle's centre is 5. Which statement describes the resulting solid?

options.text: A ring tube of radius 3 whose centreline lies on a circle of radius 5 about the axis
A solid disc of radius 5 carrying a circular hole of radius 3 punched through it
options.misconception: believes the two radii describe an outer disc and a punched hole rather than a swept tube

options.text: A sphere of radius 5 with a ball of radius 3 removed from its centre instead
options.misconception: believes the sweep of a circle about a distant axis removes material

options.text: A cylinder of radius 5 of height 3, which is what a circular sweep produces
options.misconception: believes revolving a circle about a line gives a straight-sided solid

questions.explanation: Revolving a circle of radius 3 about a coplanar axis 5 units from its centre sweeps out a tube whose cross-section is that circle, so 3 is the radius of the tube and 5 is the radius of the circle traced by the tube's centreline. That is exactly the geometry of a ring torus, and it is neither a disc with a hole nor a cylinder, since the cross-section does not stay fixed along the axis direction.
questions.hint: Ask what cross-section a plane through the axis cuts out of the solid.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.learningObjective: identify a quadric surface from the signs of its squared terms
questions.stem: The surface given by x squared over 9 minus y squared over 16 minus z squared over 16 equal to 1 has how many sheets, and along which axis is it symmetric?

options.text: Two sheets, because the single positive term forces the surface away from the origin
One sheet, because the single positive term gives a connected waist around the axis
options.misconception: believes a single positive squared term always produces one connected sheet

options.text: Two sheets, and the sheets are joined along the y-axis where the negatives vanish
options.misconception: believes the sheets meet where the negative squared terms drop out

options.text: One sheet, and the cross-section at the origin is a circle of radius 4
options.misconception: believes a cross-section through the origin must be a circle of some radius

questions.explanation: With one squared term positive and the others negative, the left-hand side is at most one only when the positive term is at least one, which forces the surface to stay away from the origin along the axis of that positive term, producing two disjoint sheets. One positive and one negative term would give a single connected sheet, and no cross-section at the origin exists here because the equation fails there.
questions.hint: Ask what happens at the origin, and whether the two sides can join.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.learningObjective: apply the matrix of a rotation about a coordinate axis
questions.stem: A vector ⟨1, 0⟩ in the plane is rotated 90 degrees counterclockwise about the origin. What vector results? Report the two components, separated by a comma.
questions.explanation: The rotation matrix for a right angle counterclockwise is the matrix with rows 0, minus 1 and 1, 0, and applying it to ⟨1, 0⟩ gives the first component 0 times 1 minus 1 times 0, which is 0, and the second component 1 times 1 plus 0 times 0, which is 1, so the result is ⟨0, 1⟩. The length is unchanged at 1 and the vector has turned a quarter turn, as required.
questions.hint: Write down the quarter-turn matrix and multiply it by the vector.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.learningObjective: apply the matrix that reflects across a line in the plane
questions.stem: Reflect the point (2, 5) across the line y equal to x. What is the x-coordinate of the image? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Reflection across the line y equal to x exchanges the two coordinates, so the image is (5, 2) and the x-coordinate asked for is 5. The matrix is the one with rows 0, 1 and 1, 0, and it is its own inverse, so applying it twice returns the original point, which is the defining property of a reflection. The image also lies the same distance from the mirror line as the original.
questions.hint: Reflection across the diagonal line exchanges the two coordinates.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.learningObjective: compute the surface area of a torus from its two radii
questions.stem: A torus has tube radius 3 and centreline radius 5. What is its surface area? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The surface area of a ring torus is 4π² times the product of the two radii, so with tube radius 3 and centreline radius 5 it is 4π² times 15, that is 60π², about 1776.53. Sweeping the tube's circumference 2π times 5 along the centreline and multiplying by Pappus on the generating circle's area would compute a volume instead, which is the trap of confusing the two quantities here.
questions.hint: Multiply four π squared by the product of the tube radius and the centreline radius.

questions.learningObjective: predict the effect of a shear on coordinates
questions.stem: The matrix with rows 1, 2 and 0, 1 is applied to the vector (1, 3). What is the first component of the result? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Applying the matrix gives a first component of 1 times 1 plus 2 times 3, which is 7, and a second component of 0 times 1 plus 1 times 3, which is 3. A shear tilts one axis toward the other while leaving the other axis fixed, and the check is that the matrix has determinant one, so areas are preserved even though lengths and angles are not.
questions.hint: Multiply the matrix by the vector, remembering to take the sum of two products per component.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.learningObjective: recover the centre and radius of a sphere from a general equation
questions.stem: The sphere x squared plus y squared plus z squared minus 6x minus 8z equal to 3 has what radius? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Completing the square in x and in z gives (x minus 3) squared plus (z minus 4) squared equal to 3 plus 9 plus 16, that is 28, and y squared is already complete, so the centre is (3, 0, 4) and the radius is the root of 28, about 5.2915. The halves of the linear coefficients give the centre coordinates, and the shift is added to the right-hand side, not subtracted.
questions.hint: Complete the square in each coordinate, then read the radius off the right-hand side.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.learningObjective: apply a scaling transformation with different factors on each axis
questions.stem: A point (3, −1) is scaled by 2 in the horizontal direction and by 5 in the vertical direction. What is the x-coordinate of the image? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: A scaling multiplies each coordinate by its own factor, so the horizontal coordinate becomes 3 times 2, which is 6, and the vertical becomes minus 1 times 5, which is −5, giving the image (6, −5). Applying a single uniform factor to both coordinates would be a dilation by that factor, whereas a per-axis scaling is what the problem specifies and it does not preserve angles.
questions.hint: Multiply the horizontal coordinate by the horizontal factor only.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.topic: Completing the square for a sphere
questions.learningObjective: rewrite a general sphere equation in centre-radius form
questions.stem: A sphere is given by x squared plus y squared plus z squared minus 6x minus 8z equal to 3. Which completed form identifies its centre and radius?

options.text: (x minus 3) squared plus y squared plus (z minus 4) squared equal to 28, centre (3, 0, 4)
(x minus 3) squared plus y squared plus (z minus 4) squared equal to 3, centre (3, 0, 4)
options.misconception: believes completing the square leaves the right-hand side untouched

options.text: (x plus 3) squared plus y squared plus (z plus 4) squared equal to 28, centre (3, 0, 4)
options.misconception: believes the sign of the linear term is kept when the square is completed

options.text: (x minus 3) squared plus y squared plus (z minus 4) squared equal to 61, centre (3, 0, 4)
options.misconception: believes the halves of the linear coefficients must be added to the right-hand side

questions.explanation: Writing x squared minus 6x as (x minus 3) squared minus 9 and z squared minus 8z as (z minus 4) squared minus 16 moves 9 and 16 to the right-hand side, giving 3 + 9 + 16 = 28. The centre is therefore (3, 0, 4) with radius the root of 28, about 5.29, and the sign of the linear coefficient reverses because the half is subtracted inside the bracket.
questions.hint: Complete the square in each coordinate, then collect the moved constants on the right.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.learningObjective: write a translation as a matrix acting on homogeneous coordinates
questions.stem: Which matrix translates every point by the vector (2, 5) when it acts on a column of homogeneous coordinates (x, y, 1)?

options.text: Rows 1, 0, 2 and 0, 1, 5 and 0, 0, 1, so the shift sits in the last column
Rows 1, 0, 0 and 0, 1, 0 and 2, 5, 1, so the shift sits in the last row
options.misconception: believes the shift must occupy the last row of the matrix

options.text: Rows 1, 2, 0 and 5, 1, 0 and 0, 0, 1, so the shift scales the coordinates
options.misconception: believes a translation is achieved by putting the shift into the diagonal

options.text: Rows 2, 0, 0 and 0, 5, 0 and 0, 0, 1, so the shift multiplies the coordinates
options.misconception: believes a translation is a scaling by the shift amounts

questions.explanation: The linear part of the matrix must be the identity so that the coordinates pass through unchanged, and the only way an affine map adds a constant is by adding a multiple of the last row, which is the constant 1 in the homogeneous column, giving the extra entries in the last column. The bottom row must stay 0, 0, 1 so that the final coordinate of the product is again 1 and the map can be repeated.
questions.hint: The last row fixes the homogeneous coordinate, so the shift must enter elsewhere.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.learningObjective: evaluate a work integral from a force expressed as a function of position
questions.stem: A force of magnitude 3x squared newtons acts along the x-axis at position x, and the object moves from x equal to 0 to x equal to 4. What work is done, in joules? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Work is the integral of force with respect to displacement, so it is the integral from 0 to 4 of 3x squared, which is 3 times 64 over 3, that is 64 joules. Multiplying the force at the endpoint by the displacement would give 48 times 4, which ignores that the force varies, and the check is that the average force over the interval is 64 over 4, or 16, which sits between 0 and 48 as it must.
questions.hint: Integrate the force with respect to the displacement variable, not the other way round.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.learningObjective: obtain velocity by differentiating a position function
questions.stem: A point moves so that its position is (t squared, 3t). At t equal to 2, first report its velocity, then report its speed.

options.text: The velocity is (4, 3) and the speed is 5
The velocity is (4, 3) and the speed is 7
options.misconception: believes the speed is the sum of the magnitudes of the velocity components

options.text: The velocity is (2, 3) and the speed is 5
options.misconception: believes differentiating t squared gives the parameter rather than twice it

options.text: The velocity is (2, 3) and the speed is 7
options.misconception: believes the position itself is the velocity and speed adds the components

Taking the sum of the component magnitudes would give 7, which is a taxicab length rather than the straight-line rate of travel, and a check on a step of 0.001 in t shows a distance travelled of about 0.005, matching the speed.
questions.hint: Differentiate the position to get the velocity, then take the magnitude of that vector.

questions.topic: Springs and a factor of one half
questions.learningObjective: evaluate the work needed to stretch a spring from its natural length
questions.stem: A spring has stiffness constant 50 newtons per metre and is stretched from its natural length to 2 metres. Which integral and which value give the work done?

options.text: The integral of 50x from 0 to 2, which evaluates to 100 joules
The integral of 50x from 0 to 2, which evaluates to 200 joules
options.misconception: believes the work equals the final force times the final extension

options.text: The integral of 25x from 0 to 2, which evaluates to 50 joules
options.misconception: believes the force of a spring is half the stiffness times the extension

options.misconception: believes the force of a spring does not grow with the extension

Treating the force as constant at its final value 100 over the whole 2 metres would double the answer, and halving the stiffness inside the integral would halve it wrongly.
questions.hint: Recognise that the force grows with the extension, so the integral matters.

questions.learningObjective: compute the average value of a function on an interval

questions.explanation: The average value is one over the length of the interval times the integral, and the interval has length 3 while the integral of x squared from 0 to 3 is 9, so the average is 3. questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.learningObjective: describe what a per-axis scaling does and what it fails to preserve
questions.stem: A figure is scaled by a factor of 2 horizontally and a factor of 5 vertically. What does the transformation do, and what does it not preserve?

options.text: It stretches coordinates along each axis, changing lengths and angles but not straightness
It multiplies every distance by the same amount, so all lengths grow by a factor of 10
options.misconception: believes a per-axis scaling is a uniform dilation by the product of the factors

options.text: It slides the figure without resizing it, since scaling only moves a shape about
options.misconception: believes any linear map is a translation of the figure

options.text: It turns the figure about the origin, since any change of components is a rotation
options.misconception: believes a change of scale can be expressed as a change of direction

questions.explanation: Scaling multiplies each coordinate by its own factor, so the figure is stretched by 2 in one direction and 5 in the other, which changes lengths and angles but keeps lines straight and keeps parallel lines parallel. A uniform dilation would be the special case of equal factors, and neither a translation nor a rotation changes coordinate magnitudes in this way, since both fix the length of every segment.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to a slope when the horizontal and vertical scales differ.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.learningObjective: describe the geometric effect of a shear transformation
questions.stem: A shear tilts the figure in one direction while leaving one axis unchanged. Which property does a shear preserve?

options.text: Areas, because the matrix of a shear has determinant equal to one
Angles, because a shear changes only the positions and not the directions
options.misconception: believes tilting the figure leaves the angles between its edges alone

options.text: Lengths, because a shear rotates each edge without stretching it
options.misconception: believes a shear is a rotation applied to each edge separately

options.text: Perpendicularity, because a shear keeps right angles as right angles
options.misconception: believes perpendicular lines stay perpendicular under a shear

questions.explanation: A shear has a unit lower-left entry and an identity diagonal, so its determinant is one and areas are preserved exactly, which is what makes it an area-preserving distortion. Angles and lengths are not preserved, because a horizontal segment is stretched by the shear while a vertical one is not, and a right angle between them is generally destroyed. The same determinant-one reasoning does not extend to right angles, which depend on the metric rather than the area.
questions.hint: Compute the determinant of a shear matrix and see what it tells you.

questions.learningObjective: describe the matrix of a reflection and its defining property
questions.stem: A reflection in the plane is represented by a 2 by 2 matrix. Which property must that matrix have?

It has determinant equal to one, so reflections preserve area like rotations do
options.misconception: believes every plane transformation has determinant one

options.text: It has determinant equal to minus one, so it reverses the orientation of the plane
options.misconception: believes the sign of the determinant records orientation rather than area scaling

options.text: It is its own transpose, so its rows and its columns are the same list of numbers
options.misconception: believes reflection is a symmetric matrix operation

The matrix of a reflection across the line y equal to x is the one with rows 0, 1 and 1, 0, which is symmetric but is not its own inverse, since squaring it gives the identity rather than the matrix itself.
questions.hint: Ask what physically happens when the same reflection is applied twice in a row.

questions.learningObjective: identify the matrix of a rotation about a coordinate axis
questions.stem: Which matrix rotates a point in the plane counterclockwise about the origin through an angle θ?

Rows sin θ, cos θ and minus cos θ, sin θ, which is the same map in the opposite sense
options.misconception: believes the two arrangements of sine and cosine describe one rotation

options.text: Rows cos θ, sin θ and minus sin θ, cos θ, which is the transpose of the rotation
options.misconception: believes the transpose of a rotation matrix is also a rotation

options.text: Rows cos 2θ, minus sin 2θ and sin 2θ, cos 2θ, since the angle appears twice in a rotation

answer.exemplar: The force rises from zero at the natural length to its final value in proportion to the extension, so the force-extension graph is a straight line through the origin and the work is the area under that line, which is a triangle of the same base and half the height, giving one half of the final force times the extension.

An answer that attributes the half to a fudge factor rather than to the shape of the graph is not an explanation.

It raises the peak frequency slightly above the undamped natural frequency
options.misconception: believes damping stiffens the system and raises its natural frequency

options.text: It leaves the peak exactly at the natural frequency, since damping only sets the height
options.misconception: believes damping changes the peak height but not its location

options.text: It removes the peak entirely, so the amplitude is largest at zero driving frequency
options.misconception: believes damping destroys resonance instead of shifting it

questions.explanation: The amplitude of a driven oscillator is the driving force divided by the root of the difference between the driving term and the stiffness, squared and summed with the damping term, squared, and maximising that denominator shows the peak sits at the root of the stiffness over the mass minus a positive correction built from the damping, so damping always lowers it. The correction is a subtraction because the damping term competes with the stiffness term at the frequency where they best cancel.
questions.hint: Maximise the denominator of the amplitude formula and look at the sign of the damping correction.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.topic: Circular motion from a centripetal condition
questions.learningObjective: find a speed from a centripetal force balance
questions.stem: An object travels in a horizontal circle of radius 5 metres, and the only horizontal force on it is its weight, 9.8 newtons per kilogram, with mass 1 kilogram. What speed does it need? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The centripetal condition is that the required inward force equals the mass times the square of the speed divided by the radius, so the square of the speed is the force times the radius divided by the mass, which is 9.8 times 5, that is 49, and the speed is 7 metres per second. Multiplying instead of dividing the radius, or forgetting to take the square root, would give 49 or 24.5, neither of which is a speed.
questions.hint: Set the centripetal requirement equal to the available force and solve for the square of the speed.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.learningObjective: state how orbital speed depends on the radius of a circular orbit
questions.stem: A satellite moves in a circular orbit of radius r about a body whose gravitational parameter is fixed. How does the orbital speed vary with r?

options.text: It varies as the inverse square root of r, so a larger orbit is a slower one
It varies as the square root of r, so a larger orbit is a faster one
options.misconception: believes the gravitational force grows with the radius of the orbit

options.text: It is independent of r, since the same satellite always keeps the same speed
options.misconception: believes the speed of a satellite is a property of the satellite alone

options.text: It varies as the inverse of r, so halving the radius doubles the speed exactly
options.misconception: believes the speed is inversely proportional rather than to the square root

questions.explanation: Equating the gravitational force to the centripetal requirement gives the square of the speed equal to the gravitational parameter divided by the radius, so the speed is that quantity times the inverse square root of r, which falls as the orbit grows. The fall is gentler than inversely proportional because the radius appears in the force and the radius again in the centripetal formula, so two powers of r appear and only the net power one half survives.
questions.hint: Set the gravitational force equal to the centripetal requirement and simplify the powers of r.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.learningObjective: expose a claim about orbital speed that a conservation law forbids
questions.stem: A student claims that a satellite in a circular orbit moves faster when it is raised to a higher circular orbit. What does conservation of angular momentum and energy say?

options.text: A higher circular orbit is slower, since the speed varies as the inverse square root of the radius
A higher circular orbit is faster, since greater radius implies a greater orbital speed
options.misconception: believes orbital speed grows with the radius of the orbit

options.text: Both orbits have the same speed, since the same satellite cannot change its speed at all
options.misconception: believes the speed of a satellite is fixed by the satellite itself

options.text: The claim cannot be judged, since circular orbits at different radii are unrelated problems
options.misconception: believes conservation laws cannot compare two different orbits

questions.explanation: For a circular orbit the balance of gravity with the centripetal requirement fixes the speed as the root of the gravitational parameter over the radius, so raising the orbit strictly lowers the speed, and the same conclusion follows from conservation of energy because the higher orbit sits at greater potential energy and so has less kinetic energy. The student's belief is a common misreading of the fact that the higher orbit takes longer to complete, which is a period statement rather than a speed statement.
questions.hint: Use the orbital balance, then check it agrees with what energy conservation demands.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.topic: Why a translation needs affine coordinates
questions.learningObjective: explain why no matrix acting on plain coordinates can translate the plane
questions.stem: Explain why a translation of the plane cannot be carried out by a two by two matrix acting on ordinary coordinates, and what the extra coordinate supplies.

answer.exemplar: Every matrix sends the zero vector to itself, so any linear map fixes the origin and therefore cannot move it, which a translation must do; adjoining a constant coordinate equal to one lets the last row of the matrix add a fixed amount to each coordinate while the output's last coordinate stays one, so the shift can be expressed as a matrix after all.

questions.explanation: A good answer states that a matrix fixes the zero vector, so no linear map can move the origin, and then explains that the homogeneous coordinate turns an affine map into a linear one by providing the constant term. An answer that says only that translations are not linear is incomplete, since it does not say how they are represented. An answer suggesting a matrix with a nonzero first column would move the origin but would also rescale, which is a different map.
questions.hint: Ask where a matrix must send the zero vector, and compare that with what a translation does.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.learningObjective: set up the force balance that determines a terminal velocity
questions.stem: A falling object of mass m experiences weight mg downward and a drag of k v upward, where v is its speed. Which condition determines its terminal speed?

options.text: The weight equals the drag, so k v equals m g and the terminal speed is mg over k
The drag equals zero, so the terminal speed is reached when the object stops accelerating
options.misconception: believes terminal speed means the acceleration has vanished for another reason

options.text: The weight equals zero, so the terminal speed is reached in free fall with no force
options.misconception: believes terminal speed describes an object with no forces acting

options.text: The drag equals the weight times the speed, so k v equals m g v and v cancels
options.misconception: believes the speed appears on both sides of the force balance

questions.explanation: A terminal speed is where the net force vanishes, because then the acceleration is zero and the speed stops changing while remaining positive, so equating the downward weight to the upward drag gives k v equal to m g and therefore a terminal speed of mg over k. Dividing both sides by the speed as in option D would leave only the statement that k equals m g, which says nothing about any speed at all.
questions.hint: Ask what condition on the acceleration defines a steady speed, then balance the forces.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.learningObjective: rescale a spring work calculation when the stiffness changes
questions.stem: A spring of stiffness 200 newtons per metre is compressed by 0.4 metres. First report the work done, then report the work done if the stiffness were doubled to 400 newtons per metre for the same compression.

options.text: The work is 16 joules and it becomes 32 joules when the stiffness is doubled
The work is 16 joules and it becomes 64 joules when the stiffness is doubled
options.misconception: believes doubling the stiffness multiplies the work by the square of two

options.text: The work is 32 joules and it becomes 16 joules when the stiffness is doubled
options.misconception: believes a stiffer spring stores less energy at the same compression

options.text: The work is 8 joules and it stays 8 joules when the stiffness is doubled
options.misconception: believes the work depends only on the compression and not the stiffness

questions.explanation: The work is one half of the stiffness times the square of the compression, so with stiffness 200 and compression 0.4 it is 100 times 0.16, which is 16 joules, and doubling the stiffness while holding the compression fixed doubles the work to 32 joules. The dependence on the stiffness is linear rather than quadratic, so the work grows by a factor of two and not by a factor of four.
questions.hint: Use the half times stiffness times compression squared formula, then vary the stiffness alone.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.learningObjective: find the cross-sectional circle cut from a cone by a plane
questions.stem: The cone z equal to x squared plus y squared is cut by the plane z equal to 9. First report the radius of the circular cross-section, then report the area of that cross-section.

options.text: The radius is 3 and the cross-sectional area is 9π, about 28.2743
The radius is 9 and the cross-sectional area is 81π, about 254.469
options.misconception: believes the height of the plane equals the radius of the cross-section

options.text: The radius is 3 and the cross-sectional area is 18, about 18
options.misconception: believes the area of a circle of radius 3 is twice the radius

options.text: The radius is 3 and the cross-sectional area is 3, taking the plane's height as the area
options.misconception: believes a cross-section inherits the height of the cutting plane

questions.explanation: On the plane z = 9 the equation of the cone gives x squared plus y squared equal to 9, which is a circle of radius 3 centred on the z-axis, and its area is π times 9, that is 9π, about 28.2743. The height of the cutting plane fixes the radius because of the way the cone opens, and a unit is being used for the coefficient in the cone's equation, so the numbers are in consistent units throughout.
questions.hint: Substitute the plane's height into the cone's equation and read off the radius.
